section.heading: Your Situation Is Probably One We've Handled.
section.subline: Dementia? Post-ICU? A first-time grandparent? A strict Brahmin kitchen with onion-and-garlic-free rules? A family that has already tried two helpers this year. We take the calls other agencies return.

stories.title: A Mother's First Day Home, Fed By Team
stories.alt: A home cook preparing a warm South Indian meal
stories.body:
The call came on a Tuesday morning. A new mother, home from the hospital for barely 36 hours, needed someone who could walk into her kitchen and cook — not just heat up food, but actually cook the way her mother did. Idlis that were soft, sambar with the right amount of tamarind, rasam that tasted like home.

We had a cook in Kottivakkam who had spent five years cooking for families along the OMR corridor. She understood South Indian vegetarian kitchens — the kind where the kadai is seasoned and the filter coffee is non-negotiable. We sent her profile that same afternoon. The family approved after a phone call.

By Thursday, the cook was in the kitchen. By Sunday, the new mother was eating three proper meals a day instead of skipping lunch. The cook adapted to the family's spice level without being asked, cleaned the cooking area before leaving each day, and even learned to make the specific type of upma the baby's grandmother preferred.

Five years later, she's still with them.

This is what cooking placement means to us. Not just finding someone who can cook — but finding someone who cooks the way your family eats. Whether it's a daily South Indian kitchen, a pure vegetarian Brahmin household with no-onion-no-garlic rules, or a family that wants North Indian rotis alongside their curries, the right cook changes the rhythm of an entire home.

The mother told us later: 'I didn't realise how much I was running on empty until someone else was in the kitchen.' That's the gap we fill.

stories.title: From NICU To Garden Smiles Again
stories.alt: A newborn baby sleeping peacefully under care
stories.body:
The baby came home from the NICU on a Saturday. Twelve days in the hospital — premature, fragile, and now suddenly back in a house that was too quiet and too unprepared. The parents were running on adrenaline and fear. Every sound the baby made felt like an alarm.

We placed a newborn care specialist the following Monday. She had twelve years of experience with NICU graduates — babies who needed careful feeding, careful positioning, and careful monitoring. She knew how to swaddle a baby who startled easily, how to read the early signs of reflux, how to set up a feeding schedule that didn't exhaust the mother.

She didn't just care for the baby. She taught the parents. How to hold a preemie during feeding. How to do tummy time safely. When to call the paediatrician and when to wait. By the end of the second week, the mother told us she had slept a full five hours for the first time since the birth.

By the time the baby was four months old, the garden where the parents had taken their first nervous walks was now the place where the baby smiled at the flowers.

Newborn care isn't just about the baby. It's about a family finding its footing during the most vulnerable weeks of their lives. Whether it's a NICU graduate or a first-time parent who needs guidance through those first 40 days, the right person makes the difference between survival and actually enjoying it.

The father's words stayed with us: 'She gave us our confidence back.'

stories.title: Grandfather's 80th, Our Hands
stories.alt: An elderly gentleman smiling with his caregiver
stories.body:
It was Grandfather's 80th birthday. Three generations under one roof, but the one person he wanted to be there — his eldest son — was in Toronto. The family had tried two helpers that year. One left after a week. The other was kind but had no experience with a man who used a walking frame and refused to admit he needed help.

We placed a live-in attendant in Perungudi. She had cared for elderly patients for eight years — not just physically, but emotionally. She understood that dignity mattered more than efficiency. She helped Grandfather walk to the bathroom without making him feel like a patient. She sat with him during the afternoons when the house was quiet and the TV didn't fill the silence.

By the second week, Grandfather was eating meals at the table again instead of in his room. By the third week, he was telling her stories about his days at the bank. She learned to make his tea exactly the way he liked it — strong, with just a little sugar.

On the morning of his birthday, the family video-called Toronto. Grandfather was sitting in his chair, clean-shaven, wearing his favourite shirt, with the attendant quietly adjusting the pillow behind him. His son cried.

'Elderly care' is a phrase that sounds clinical. But what it actually means is: someone who sees your father or grandfather as a person, not a task list. Someone who keeps the morning routine going, the tea ritual going, the stories going. Someone who ensures that the person who once held everything together doesn't feel like they've been left behind.

That's what we mean when we say we handle the calls other agencies return.

stories.title: A Hip Surgery, Home Safe
stories.alt: A patient being assisted during recovery
stories.body:
Six hours after hip replacement surgery, the hospital said he could go home. The family wasn't ready. No hospital bed, no bed rail, no one in the house trained to help a 72-year-old man get from the bed to the bathroom without falling. The doctor said recovery at home was better — but only if the right care was in place.

We placed a patient care attendant within 48 hours. She had four years of post-surgical recovery experience — hip replacements, knee surgeries, post-cardiac care. She knew the exercises the physiotherapist prescribed. She knew how to assist with bathing without making it feel like a loss of independence. She kept the medication chart and made sure nothing was missed.

The first week was hard. There was a night when he couldn't get comfortable and the attendant stayed up with him, adjusting his position until he slept. There was a morning when she caught a slight swelling in his ankle and called the doctor before it became a problem.

By week three, he was walking to the dining table with a walker. By week five, he was walking to the gate. The physiotherapist said his recovery was ahead of schedule.

His daughter told us: 'We could focus on being his family again instead of being his nurses.'

That's what patient care at home actually means. It's not just a helper — it's someone who understands the medical routine, respects the patient's dignity, and gives the family room to breathe during the hardest weeks. Whether it's post-surgery recovery, post-ICU care, or long-term bedside assistance, the right attendant transforms the home from a place of worry into a place of healing.
